content:
The argument from suffering is the oldest objection to belief in a merciful God: if he is merciful, why do children suffer, and why do the powerful hurt the weak? It is also the objection that moves people most, because it usually comes from someone who has been hurt. An answer that sounds like a slogan insults the question.

These six points set out what the Islamic sources say, and where they stop. They do not claim to solve the problem. They claim that the sources take it seriously, give a coherent place for pain, and put the blame for human cruelty where it belongs. For related questions see fate and free will, why the universe needs a creator and morality without God.

God "created death and life to test you as to which of you is best in deed" (67:2). "Do the people think that they will be left to say, 'We believe' and they will not be tried?" (29:2). The Quran also says, "We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger and a loss of wealth and lives and fruits" (2:155).[1]

The idea of a test is the Quran's first answer, and it is incomplete as an answer to a child's illness, because a child is not being tested for anything. Scholars add that the test falls on those around the child, on parents, doctors and neighbours, who are asked to respond with mercy. That reply helps with the actions of people. It does not explain every pain.

A reader should be careful how the verses are used. They are said to a person who is bearing pain, to ask what she will do with it. They do not say that a person who inflicts pain is doing God's testing, or that a victim of abuse was tested and failed. The man who beats his wife or his child is not a test sent from heaven. He is a wrongdoer, and the same Quran says that he will answer for it. Telling a victim that her abuse was a test, and that she should be patient, mistakes a verse about endurance for a licence for harm.

Strength: moderate. The verses are firm, and the answer covers some suffering and not all.

The prophets are shown in pain. Job said, "adversity has touched me, and You are the most merciful of the merciful" (21:83). Jonah, in the belly of the fish, called out within the darkness (21:87). The Quran says that the earlier prophets and their followers "were touched by poverty and hardship and were shaken until even their messenger said, 'When is the help of Allah?'" (2:214).[2]

So the sources do not treat suffering as a sign that God has withdrawn, or that the sufferer has done wrong. A prophet cries out and God answers, and in 2:214 even the messenger asks when the help will come. The tradition does not demand that the sufferer keep calm.

Strength: firm. This is the strongest reply to the claim that pain disproves mercy: the Quran's heroes suffer, and the Quran says so.

God says, "with hardship will be ease" (94:5 to 6), "Allah will bring about, after hardship, ease" (65:7) and "Allah does not charge a soul except with that within its capacity" (2:286).[3] The last of these has been read to mean that a person is accountable only for what she can bear and do.

A critic may say that the verses promise too much, since some people die in pain and never see ease. The Muslim answer places the ease in the next life as well as this one, and the next entry sets out why. A reader who does not accept the next life will not be moved by it, and the entry does not pretend otherwise.

The verses do not tell the sufferer to feel better, and they do not say that the hardship is small. They say that ease will come with it, and they leave the hardship hard. A person may therefore believe the promise and still weep, as the Prophet ﷺ wept at his son's grave. The tradition does not ask her to choose between the two.

Strength: moderate. The promise is clear, and the reply to "some never see ease" rests on the afterlife.

In a report in Sahih Muslim, God says, "O My servants, I have forbidden oppression for Myself and have made it forbidden amongst you, so do not oppress one another."[4] The Quran says that "Allah does not do injustice, even as much as an atom's weight" (4:40) and that he "forbids immorality and bad conduct and oppression" (16:90).[5]

The Quran does not ascribe a father's beating or a trafficker's trade to God. It ascribes them to the person who does them, who will answer for it: "whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it" (99:8). The answer to "why did God let a man do that" is that God gave people choice, and harm is the misuse of it. That is the free-will reply, and it is the reply most people find hardest, because it does not undo the harm.

The sources add that wrongs are settled. The Prophet ﷺ said that whoever has oppressed another person, in his reputation or in anything else, should beg his forgiveness before the Day of Resurrection, when there will be no money to compensate for wrong deeds. If the oppressor has good deeds, they will be taken from him in proportion to his oppression, and if he has none, the sins of the oppressed will be loaded on him.[6] Many of the wronged will never see this on earth. The report says that it will be seen. For a believer, the harm is not left unanswered. For a person who does not believe in the next life, the report gives no comfort, and the entry does not claim that it does.

Strength: moderate. The free-will reply is old and strong, and it leaves the question of why so much harm is allowed.

The Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said that no fatigue, disease, sorrow, sadness, hurt or distress befalls a Muslim, even the prick of a thorn, but God expiates some of his sins for it.[7] He also said that a Muslim is a brother of a Muslim, so he should not oppress him, and that whoever relieves his brother of a discomfort, God will relieve him of the discomforts of the Day of Resurrection.[8]

Two things follow. Suffering is not wasted: it carries weight in God's accounting. And the believer is not allowed to watch it. He is told to relieve it. A faith that said only "be patient" would be open to the charge of excusing the world. This one ties patience to action, and puts the burden of action on the one who can help.

There is a further point in the second report. The Prophet ﷺ did not say that a believer should leave an oppressor to God and look away. He said that the oppressed should not be handed over to an oppressor, and that anyone who helps his brother in need will be helped. The duty is placed on the one who sees the harm, and it is not satisfied by sympathy alone.

Strength: moderate. The reports are authentic. They give pain meaning for the believer. They do not tell the unbeliever why pain exists.

The Quran says of God, "He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned" (21:23).[9] The verse is sometimes used to end a discussion. Read with the others, it says that a creature cannot require God to explain himself in full, and that the creature remains accountable for what she does.

The honest position is that the Islamic sources give a place for pain, a reason to endure it, a ban on causing it and a duty to relieve it, and that they do not give a full explanation of why there is so much of it. A reader who wants a full explanation will not find one here. Some Muslim theologians said that God's wisdom is beyond human grasp, and others argued that this is the best world that could be. Neither is a proof, and both are held by faith.

It is also fair to say what the objection has shown. Any account of a merciful God must face the pain of children, and the Islamic account does so by appeal to freedom, to the next life and to the limits of what a creature can know. Those who find the appeal sufficient are not being foolish, and those who do not are not being wicked. Both can say that the pain is real and that it is wrong. The Quran says the same, and it asks the believer to act on it.

Strength: firm that the sources stop here. They give the believer words for the pain and a task in the face of it.

The bottom line

The argument from suffering is serious, and the Islamic sources treat it so. Of the six points, one is firm and decisive against a particular form of the objection: the Quran's own heroes suffer, and the Quran says that pain is not proof of God's absence. Four are moderate: the test, the promise of ease, the free-will reply, and the meaning given to pain. The last is a limit: the sources give no full explanation.

A person who has been hurt, especially as a child, is entitled to say that the answers do not reach what happened. The tradition lets her say so. It also asks the community to act where it can, since relieving a brother's distress is a duty and not a favour. Allāhu aʿlam.

Notes

  1. Quran 67:2, 29:2 and 2:155, Saheeh International translation, read on the Quran.com API. That scholars add the test to those around the sufferer is stated from general knowledge, and no source is cited for it.
  2. Quran 21:83, 21:87 and 2:214, Saheeh International.
  3. Quran 94:5 to 6, 65:7 and 2:286, Saheeh International.
  4. Sahih Muslim 2577, hadith qudsi, report of Abū Dharr; read in the English text of the hadith-api edition (book 45, hadith 70 there); the printed page was not checked.
  5. Quran 4:40 and 16:90, Saheeh International. Quran 99:8 is cited in the text, same translation.
  6. Sahih al-Bukhari 2449, report of Abū Hurayra, on settling wrongs before the Day of Resurrection (read in the English text of the hadith-api edition).
  7. Sahih al-Bukhari 5641, report of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī and Abū Hurayra (read in the English text of the hadith-api edition).
  8. Sahih al-Bukhari 2442, report of ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar (same source).
  9. Quran 21:23, Saheeh International. The remark that some theologians said God's wisdom is beyond human grasp and others that this is the best possible world is a general statement of the tradition, and no work is cited for it.
